title: ZTE Secret of Agentic Engineering
lesson_subtitle: Understand the North Star of Agentic Coding where your codebase ships itself. Progress from in loop, to out loop, to ZTE.

tactic.name: Target Zero-Touch Engineering
tactic.one_liner: Build your out-loop system so reliable that human review becomes a bottleneck, not a safety net — then drop the review: presence goes from two touchpoints (prompt + review) to one (prompt only), and work flows directly from prompt to production.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: TAC-1 asked you to stop coding; TAC-7 asks you to stop reviewing — the last place engineers feel indispensable. Dan names the reaction in-lesson: 'I know you're probably O-faced right now... Dan, absolutely no way, that's crazy. This isn't a real production application.' He agrees the demo app is a toy, then argues that objection misses the point: ZTE is a North Star you earn one problem class at a time (chores → bugs → features), and it only becomes available to engineers who invested in the agentic layer deeply enough to discover their review adds no value. It is 'YOLO mode for your AI developer workflows... maximum confidence mode' — deliberately provocative, deliberately gated (in the repo, the ZTE workflow literally refuses to run unless 'ZTE' is typed in uppercase).
tactic.course_page_definition: Zero-Touch Engineering is the third level of agentic coding beyond in-loop and out-loop, where your presence KPI drops from two touchpoints (prompt and review) to just one (prompt only). At this level, you witness something most engineers dismiss as impossible - a codebase that nearly runs itself. Your agents ship end-to-end with such reliability that human review becomes a bottleneck, not a safety net, allowing work to flow directly from prompt to production.
daily_actions_from_course_card: Build parallel agent pipelines using isolated environments
Scale from single agent to multi-agent workflows
Create isolated environments for simultaneous execution
Go from PITER to PITE with one prompt agentic workflows
Build ADWs so great your review step becomes irrelevant

mission: Collect the dividends of the complete end-to-end out-loop system built across TAC 1–6: hand five net-new pieces of work to the agentic layer and watch it plan, build, test, review, and document in parallel; scale beyond one agent with git-worktree isolation; add compute knobs (model sets); then confront the moment when you — the reviewer — become the bottleneck, and meet the third level of the Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale: Zero-Touch Engineering. Finally, receive the course's secret: none of this was ever about the SDLC — it's about composable agentic primitives that solve any engineering problem class.

velocity_scale.name: Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale (on-screen slide at 1:40)
velocity_scale.level1_in_loop: In-loop agentic coding: you prompt interactively inside an agentic coding tool, watch, iterate, retest. Where most engineers operate. Presence is continuous. Dan: 'In-loop agentic coding is the lowest hanging fruit. Do not remain here.'
velocity_scale.level2_out_loop: Out-loop: your engineering is templated into ADWs fired by triggers (GitHub issues → webhook). You appear exactly twice — at the prompt and at the review. 'The best out-loop agentic coders have a presence of two.' Out-loop systems beat out-of-the-box agentic tools because they contain YOUR engineering practices and workflows.
velocity_scale.level3_zte: Zero-Touch Engineering: presence drops to one (the prompt). The pipeline plans, builds, tests, reviews, documents, and ships to production with no human review. PITER loses its R and becomes PITE. Earned per problem class, not switched on globally.
velocity_scale.not_binary: Dan repeatedly guards against black-and-white reading: 'It's not in loop versus out loop. It's in loop moving toward out loop' (9:42), and mid-demo he deliberately goes back in-loop to review the drag-and-drop PR — 'think in the gray.'

piter_to_pite.recap: PITER (from TAC-4, AFK agents): Prompt input → Trigger → Environment → Review. In TAC-7 the prompt input is GitHub issues, the trigger is a webhook (or 20-second cron poll), the environment is a dedicated always-on machine (Dan's Mac mini) plus per-run git worktrees, and the review is GitHub issue comments + uploaded screenshots + PRs.
piter_to_pite.the_drop: ZTE removes the R: 'You'll drop yourself off the end of the out-loop PITER framework and it becomes PITE, not PITER. You'll drop off the review' (31:19–31:26; the transcript mis-hears it as "Pete not Peter"). The course card states it as a daily action: 'Go from PITER to PITE with one prompt agentic workflows.'

secret.statement: The secret of Tactical Agentic Coding: it's not about the software developer lifecycle at all. It's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class. (Stated twice verbatim, 45:58–46:10.)
secret.sdlc_demoted: 'The software developer lifecycle is powerful, but it's a remnant of the past... It is not the optimal way to run software with agents' (46:26). Plan/build/test/review/document was 'a package for me to deliver a message to you' — one arbitrary arrangement of primitives. 'There is no one way to do this. The one way is the way that ships in your codebase.'
secret.primitives_slide: The 46:05 slide 'The Secret: Composable Agentic Primitives' draws three columns: Agentic Primitives (ADWs, Templates, Plans, Architecture, Tests, Documentation, Types, Standard Out, Tools, Prompt, Model, Context) → ADW steps (Plan, Build, Test, Review, Document, Deploy) → Composed Workflows (Plan→Build→Test, Build→Review→Deploy, Test→Document, ANY WORKFLOW).
secret.bridge_to_tac8: Lesson 8 blows this open: 'The primitives are the atoms of agentic engineering. Master them and you can build any molecular structure you need' (51:37) — revisiting the atoms, then compositions across codebase types (web app, CLI tools, notebooks).

core_concepts.name: Collecting dividends from the agentic layer
core_concepts.plain_english: The lesson opens by cashing in on everything built in TAC 1–6: five net-new pieces of work (three features, a chore, a bug) are handed to the agentic layer as GitHub issues and shipped end-to-end while Dan reviews the codebase. The point is leverage realized: 'I parallelized myself across five features.'
core_concepts.dan_words: "Let's collect the incredible dividends from our complete end to end Outloop agentic system... once you've built the system that builds the system, it's going to pay you back massively."
core_concepts.misconception: That this is a new build. Almost nothing in the demo is new machinery — it is TAC-4's PITER + TAC-5's closed loops + TAC-6's focused agents, now running all at once, in parallel, on real work.

core_concepts.name: The three levels: in-loop → out-loop → ZTE
core_concepts.plain_english: A named scale for how present you are in the work. In-loop: you drive interactively. Out-loop: systems drive; you show up at prompt and review (presence 2). ZTE: you show up at the prompt only (presence 1). The lesson's arc is earning the right to move right on this scale.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There are three levels: in loop, out loop, and one additional level that we're going to break down in this lesson... first we're in the loop, next we're out the loop, and then we're doing ZTE — zero touch engineering."
core_concepts.misconception: Treating the scale as a switch instead of a gradient. Dan: 'This isn't black and white... It's in loop moving toward out loop. One day at a time.' He goes back in-loop on camera to review the drag-and-drop PR.

core_concepts.name: Git worktrees: parallel agents on one device
core_concepts.plain_english: Every ADW run gets its own complete copy of the repo at trees/<adw_id>/ via git worktree (branched from origin/main), its own git branch, its own .ports.env, and its own backend/frontend ports (9100–9114 / 9200–9214, hashed from the ADW ID, 15 concurrent slots). That's what lets five pipelines run simultaneously without stepping on each other — and you can jump into any of them with `code trees/<id>`.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We've adjusted all of our workflows to create their own isolated trees... In every tree, the application exists for a specific agent to build in. This is the easiest way to parallelize your workflows."
core_concepts.misconception: Fixating on worktrees as THE answer. Dan pre-empts: 'It doesn't matter that you use Git work trees... individual VMs, Docker containers — I don't care how you scale up your agent environments, it only matters that you can.' (The repo even ships an E2B cloud-sandbox proof-of-concept in adws/adw_tests/sandbox_poc.py.)

core_concepts.name: Environment setup is itself an agent task (/install_worktree)
core_concepts.plain_english: A worktree isn't usable until it's installed like an engineer would install it: copy .env files, append port config, copy .mcp.json and playwright config and rewrite their paths to absolute, uv sync, bun install, reset the database. ADW does this by running the /install_worktree slash command inside the new worktree, passing worktree path + both ports as arguments.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The work tree sets up every piece that we need to operate the codebase in a dedicated directory... We're installing as if we, the engineer, were operating. This is critical. Some type of configuration format like this is going to be really important."
core_concepts.misconception: Hand-waving environment setup. If agents can't reproduce your dev environment from scratch, parallel isolation dies at step zero — this command IS the 'engineer onboarding doc' turned executable.

core_concepts.name: The ADW state object (adw_state.json)
core_concepts.plain_english: Each run persists a small JSON at agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json with exactly ten fields: adw_id, issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class, worktree_path, backend_port, frontend_port, model_set, all_adws. Every phase loads it, adds what it learned, saves it — that's how independent scripts chain into one pipeline, how you resume/replay a run, and how ship validates that every prior phase actually happened.
core_concepts.dan_words: "To combat some of the state management issues that you're going to run into, we do have this state.json object... expect to have to add some type of state object inside your dedicated agent environments. This truly frees your agent to do one thing extraordinarily well with all the context it needs, and it lets you jump in and replay what that agent has done."
core_concepts.misconception: Stuffing state into the agent's context window instead. The state object is code-side memory; agents stay single-purpose (TAC-6) precisely because the pipeline, not the prompt, carries the bookkeeping.

core_concepts.name: TAC-6's tactic survives the scale-up
core_concepts.plain_english: Parallelism did not merge agents into one mega-context. Each phase is still one agent running one prompt with a single purpose (sdlc_planner, sdlc_implementor, tester, reviewer, documenter, shipper) — now multiplied across worktrees.
core_concepts.dan_words: "It's also important to mention that the lesson six tactic has not been broken. This is really important for scaling. We have one agent running one prompt with a single purpose... You have more precision while other engineers are trying to stack up into one context window."
core_concepts.misconception: Believing scale requires bigger agents. TAC scales by adding more isolated small agents, not by growing one agent's context.

core_concepts.name: Model sets: a compute knob encoded as an IDK
core_concepts.plain_english: Typing 'model_set heavy' in a GitHub issue changes which model every slash command runs on. agent.py holds SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP: all 18 commands run sonnet on base; on heavy, exactly 8 escalate to opus (/implement, /resolve_failed_test, /resolve_failed_e2e_test, /document, /chore, /bug, /feature, /patch) while classification/test/review/plumbing commands stay sonnet. Same prompts, same pipeline — more compute where it pays.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We're adding a knob to our capabilities... Our model set changes the set of models that runs against our workflow... It gives us a little knob to turn to increase the compute that our workflow uses. You can encode any information dense keyword you want — you just have to make sure that your prompts recognize it and pick it up."
core_concepts.misconception: Thinking heavy = better everywhere. The map is deliberately selective: creative/implementation work escalates; deterministic parsing and classification don't. Compute allocation is itself an engineering decision you encode once.

core_concepts.name: Where the knob gets read: /classify_adw at the top of every trigger
core_concepts.plain_english: The webhook hands the raw issue/comment text to the /classify_adw agent, which returns strict JSON: {adw_slash_command, adw_id, model_set}. That's how plain English in an issue selects a workflow, resumes an existing run by ID, and sets the model set — and where the safety interlock lives: the classifier is instructed to run the ZTE workflow only if 'ZTE' is explicitly uppercase, otherwise it downgrades to plain SDLC.
core_concepts.dan_words: "If you're ever wondering where this stuff runs, you can always just type slash classify ADW... it runs right here, workflow operations, where we classify the ADW at the beginning of the workflow... We've encoded this and you can see we just use base or heavy."
core_concepts.misconception: Assuming triggers need rigid syntax. The classifier normalizes variations ('adw plan build', missing _iso suffix) — natural language in, validated enum out, with code-side validation against AVAILABLE_ADW_WORKFLOWS after.

core_concepts.name: Review = proof of value (screenshots posted to the issue)
core_concepts.plain_english: The review agent starts the app in the worktree on its allocated ports, drives it with Playwright MCP, takes 1–5 numbered screenshots of the critical paths, classifies any issues (skippable / tech_debt / blocker), and returns strict JSON. Screenshots are uploaded to a Cloudflare R2 public bucket and posted back onto the triggering GitHub issue — the agent proves the feature shipped without you leaving the review system.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Our agents took images and gave us proof that the feature has shipped... Remember what the review step answers: it's not 'does it work?' It's 'is what we built what we asked for?' (21:40)... Having a comprehensive review system is a massive, massive edge for increasing your review velocity."
core_concepts.misconception: Treating review as re-testing. Tests already ran in the test phase; review compares implementation to the SPEC. And blockers don't just fail the run — the review workflow patches blockers and re-reviews (attempt loop visible on the issue: 'attempt 1/3').

core_concepts.name: adw_sdlc_zte_iso: SDLC + ship, with hard gates
core_concepts.plain_english: ZTE = the exact same SDLC pipeline plus one more phase: ship. Gates in code: test failure aborts ('ZTE Aborted - Test phase failed'), review failure aborts, documentation failure warns but does NOT block shipping, ship failure reports. Ship itself validates that all 8 required state fields are populated, verifies the worktree, then does a manual merge in the repo root: fetch, checkout main, pull, git merge --no-ff <branch>, push origin main.
core_concepts.dan_words: "All ZTE does — this will run the exact same workflow as SDLC and then it adds one more thing... run ship... If nothing fails here, if your agents get through your engineering pipeline and they've proven to you, with great review and great tests, that the feature is working... let them ship to production. Ship does exactly what you think it does... check out main on the root repository outside of the tree, merge in the feature branch, and post success."
core_concepts.misconception: Thinking ZTE is reckless automation. It's the opposite: it only ships when every gate passes, it's uppercase-gated at the classifier, and Dan's rollout advice is to earn it on the smallest possible problem class first ('your designer is having a bad day' background-color chores).

core_concepts.name: The realization: human review becomes the bottleneck
core_concepts.plain_english: The trigger for level 3 isn't technology, it's evidence: after your templated pipeline ships the same problem class end-to-end 5, 10, 20 times with your review adding nothing, continuing to review is pure latency. Dan frames the lesson-2 KPIs as the instrument: attempts pinned at 1, size scaling up, streak increasing — then presence drops to 1.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Once you become proficient at Outloop agentic coding, you'll realize something incredible: this human in the loop model is a bottleneck. I'm not catching any bugs anymore. I'm not adding any value outside of the agentic layer. I'm going to remove the human in the loop review process for this class of problems (30:45)... You'll realize that you add no value by reviewing. In fact, you slowed things down (38:36)."
core_concepts.misconception: Hearing 'stop reviewing everything now.' The claim is scoped per problem class and evidence-gated — 90% confidence on a chore class first, 'and that number keeps going up with every tool release, every model release, every time you improve your agentic layer.'

core_concepts.name: Start small: chores → bugs → features, then it compounds
core_concepts.plain_english: The rollout path (same ladder as TAC-4, now aimed at ZTE): first ship a class of chores you know repeats — front-end text/style changes, database migrations — simple, low-effort, easy to validate. Then bugs, then features. Each success compounds belief and capability.
core_concepts.dan_words: "You don't start by shipping a full feature... First, go after chores, then go after bugs, then go after features (33:07)... Everything starts small and then it compounds. Your first agent ships a chore, your next agentic workflows start shipping bugs, then features — and then they'll do it five times, 20 times... five times in a row — and you'll realize you add no value by reviewing."
core_concepts.misconception: 'This only works on toy apps.' Dan concedes the demo is a toy and answers with the counter-narrative: the point is to be trying now, because 'if you don't invest into the agentic layer of your codebase, how will you know when agents can solve your problem class end to end with no oversight?' (37:25)

core_concepts.name: The real hurdle is belief (sprint toward the future)
core_concepts.plain_english: The lesson's closing argument is not technical: you have four options as the future arrives — run away, stand still, move toward it, or sprint. The engineer who invests a week or a few weeks in the agentic layer ends up writing one prompt and shipping to production at 90% confidence; the engineer who didn't is still sitting, waiting, iterating, retesting in-loop. 'Tell me who wins this.'
core_concepts.dan_words: "The real challenge I have for you in this course... is about your belief. You have to believe that the agentic layer is worth investing into. If you don't believe that your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked (41:15)... It's not about being right. It's about being prepared to win... Don't run toward the future, don't walk toward it, sprint into the future (49:06)."
core_concepts.misconception: Reading this as hype. Dan's actual claim is falsifiable and hedged: 'If you think that zero-touch engineering is in the far future for you, that's fine. You might be right — but it's not about being right, it's about being prepared to win.'

sdlc_iso_phases: test (unit tests + auto-resolution; E2E ALWAYS skipped inside SDLC orchestrators — hardcoded --skip-e2e)
document (feature doc in app_docs/, conditional_docs update, agentic KPI tracking)
sdlc_zte_pipeline.zte_adds: ship — validate all 8 state fields non-null, validate worktree, manual git merge --no-ff of the feature branch into main in the repo root, push origin/main, post success to the issue.

zte_gates.test_fail: aborts with 'ZTE Aborted - Test phase failed' comment
zte_gates.review_fail: aborts with 'ZTE Aborted - Review phase failed' comment
zte_gates.document_fail: warns and CONTINUES to ship ('Documentation failure shouldn't block shipping')
zte_gates.ship_fail: posts 'ZTE Failed - Ship phase failed... merge manually if needed'

sdlc_zte_pipeline.zte_uppercase_interlock: .claude/commands/classify_adw.md: 'DO NOT RUN the adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso workflows unless ZTE is EXPLICITLY uppercased. This is a dangerous workflow and it needs to be absolutely clear when we're running it. If zte is not capitalized, then run the non zte version /adw_sdlc_iso.'
sdlc_zte_pipeline.naming_note: Dan's tactic says Zero-Touch Engineering; the code's docstrings and GitHub comments say Zero Touch Execution ('Starting Zero Touch Execution (ZTE)'). Same acronym, two expansions — both appear in course artifacts.

worktree_mechanics.create: git worktree add -b <branch> trees/<adw_id> origin/main (fetch first; falls back to attaching an existing branch)
worktree_mechanics.ports: index = int(first 8 alnum chars of adw_id, base 36) % 15 → backend 9100+i, frontend 9200+i; availability-checked with socket bind, next-slot fallback; written to .ports.env (BACKEND_PORT, FRONTEND_PORT, VITE_BACKEND_URL)
worktree_mechanics.validation: three-way: state has worktree_path + directory exists + `git worktree list` knows it
worktree_mechanics.cleanup: scripts/purge_tree.sh <adw_id> [--keep-branch]; latent bug documented: worktree_ops.remove_worktree calls shutil.rmtree without importing shutil, so the manual-cleanup fallback path raises NameError (caught and returned as an error string)
worktree_mechanics.branch_naming: real committed example: chore-issue-3-adw-e2ae7fad-update-adw-docs → pattern {class}-issue-{n}-adw-{id}-{slug}; adws/README's example 'feat-456-e5f6g7h8-add-user-authentication' is stale vs the code, which matches on '-issue-{n}-' and '-adw-{id}-'

programmable_agent_invocation.retry: prompt_claude_code_with_retry: up to 3 retries, delays [1, 3, 5]s, only on retryable codes (claude_code_error, timeout, execution_error, error_during_execution)
programmable_agent_invocation.logging: every prompt saved to agents/<adw_id>/<agent_name>/prompts/<command>.txt; full session streamed to raw_output.jsonl and mirrored to .json array; result message parsed for output/session_id/is_error/cost
programmable_agent_invocation.permissions_nuance: .claude/settings.json allow/deny list (deny: git push --force, git push -f, rm -rf) governs interactive sessions; ADW runs pass --dangerously-skip-permissions, so hooks + worktree isolation + the deny-listed patterns in pre_tool_use.py are the real guardrails out-loop

trigger_mechanics.webhook: adws/adw_triggers/trigger_webhook.py — FastAPI POST /gh-webhook on port 8001; handles 'issues/opened' and 'issue_comment/created'; requires 'adw_' in the text; ignores anything containing the [ADW-AGENTS] bot identifier to prevent loops; classifies via /classify_adw; dependent workflows (build/test/review/document/ship) refuse to fire without an adw_id; responds inside GitHub's 10-second timeout by launching the workflow as a detached background process
trigger_mechanics.cron: adws/adw_triggers/trigger_cron.py — polls GitHub every 20 seconds (new issues with no comments, or latest comment exactly 'adw')
trigger_mechanics.health: GET /health runs adw_tests/health_check.py (env vars, gh auth, claude CLI) and returns parsed warnings/errors

Idea notes: witness the impossible (codebase that runs itself); invest in your agentic layer; git worktrees for agent parallelization; containerization alternatives (Docker, agent-based frameworks); scaling beyond in-loop; out-loop systems contain your engineering practices; ADW scripting layer; gradual transition to out-loop (not binary); dedicated environments for agent safety; agent multiplication through isolation; build the system that builds the system; review is especially important; Tactic #7 Target Zero-Touch Engineering (presence KPI 2 → 1); the ZTE workflow plan→build→test→review→generate→ship; THE SECRET: composable agentic primitives; composable primitives trump traditional SDLC; evolution beyond SDLC (unique compositions per org); achieve ZTE when confidence hits 90% and review becomes the bottleneck.
step_by_step_demo: (0:00–2:30) Cold open: this lesson flows differently — five net-new pieces of work handed to the agentic layer that ships end to end (plan, build, test, review, document); worktree parallelization; the third level of the velocity scale; 'a critical moment in the future where human in the loop review becomes a bottleneck, not a safety net' (2:06).

(3:05–3:30) The dedicated agent environment is live: webhook trigger running, waiting on prompts from GitHub issues (PITER's prompt input); Chrome shows the Natural Language SQL app the agents operate.

(4:00–5:50) Five issues filed back to back: #51 increase drag-and-drop drop-zone surface area (feature, adw_sdlc_iso), #52 JSON export (feature, simple high-level prompt), table random data generation (feature, mid-level prompt, model_set heavy), #54 support better models / bump to o4-mini (chore), and a CSV-export text-mismatch bug routed to the lightweight adw_patch_iso instead of full SDLC (5:22).

(5:54–7:30) All five fire back to back; the webhook terminal shows events arriving, state initialized, ports allocated per run; live comments stream onto each issue ('this is absurd levels of scale', 7:08).

(8:15–9:30) Fresh clone ritual: git clone tac-7, `claude` in yolo mode, /install, then recap of the agentic layer top-down: ADWs are 'the top level, the highest compositional unit' — new workflows adw_sdlc_iso, adw_sdlc_zte_iso, adw_ship_iso (8:52).
(10:30–11:15) Inside adw_sdlc_iso.py: regex search for the subprocess chain shows it just composes the lower-level pieces — plan, build, test (skipping e2e), review, document.
(11:17–12:30) Worktree deep-dive: every workflow creates its own isolated tree under trees/; /install_worktree runs inside it with the allocated ports and worktree path (12:06).

(12:58–13:30) `code trees/<id>` — jump into a live agent's environment mid-run; branch 'chore task issue 39 <adw-id>' visible in the status bar. 'Think in the gray... so that we can hop up to our top level and improve the agentic layer' (13:22–13:49).
(14:29–15:10) TAC-6 tactic intact (one agent, one prompt, single purpose); the state.json object tracks meta-information across phases and lets you replay what an agent did (14:44–15:06).

(15:46–18:20) Model sets: heavy run in flight for the big feature; agents.py SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP on screen (16:41) — 'heavy → opus, we are running a beefed up model' (16:59); 'think hard' IDK inside chore.md activates the reasoning model (17:25); /classify_adw is where model_set gets parsed at workflow start (17:41).
(18:14–19:20) Status sweep: JSON export in review phase; drag-and-drop implementation complete, tests passed; random-data feature still implementing on the heavy set, 11 minutes in (18:37).

(18:50–19:52) The o4-mini chore finished six minutes ago: review summary on the issue, PR with ~100 lines changed, conditional docs updated, plan + docs both linked — 'we have both ends of the software developer lifecycle.'
(21:26–22:00) Review proof: the drag-and-drop agent posts screenshots to the issue — the new drop overlay visible — 'it's not does it work, it's is what we built what we asked for' (21:40–21:51).

(22:59–24:40) Back in-loop deliberately: /in_loop_review <branch> pulls the branch, resets the DB, restarts the app, opens the browser (24:10) — 'my machine, my resources, to validate my agent's work.'
(24:48–26:00) Manual browser test of drag-and-drop on both sections; 'teach your agent how to do it once and then run it over and over and over again and scale it across your team' (24:48).

(26:00–27:00) The documentation trail: app_docs/enhance-drop-zone doc references the original spec; conditional_docs.md updated so future agents pull the right doc when they touch drag-and-drop — 'this lets our agents scale with the size of our codebase.'
(27:59–29:30) Zoom out: 'You can't vibe code this stuff' (27:59); 'when the agents arrived, something changed — we weren't just AI coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence' (29:21).

(30:45–32:30) The realization monologue: review is the bottleneck; the velocity scale completes: in-loop → out-loop → ZTE; PITER becomes PITE (31:19); 'YOLO mode... maximum confidence mode' (31:33); tactic named: Target Zero-Touch Engineering (31:50); KPIs: attempts 1, size up, streak up, presence 1 (31:56); 'the best out-loop agentic coders have a presence of two' (32:15).
(32:37–33:30) The objection handled: 'you're probably O-faced right now... this isn't a real production application' — slow down: chores first, then bugs, then features (33:07).

(33:46–35:30) ZTE mechanics: same SDLC + ship (approve/merge agentically) (33:55); demo issue #62 'Update the background color' with /chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso (34:38–34:58); initiation comment lists all six phases + auto-merge warning (35:31).

(36:24–40:40) The counter-narrative monologue: toy-app objection conceded and dismissed; 'prepare for agentic coding capabilities to go parabolic' (37:06); 'you are doing engineering work you do not have to do' (37:40); compounding (37:53); the two-engineer comparison — one prompt to production at 90% confidence vs sit/wait/iterate/retest (39:52–40:36).

(41:00–43:45) The belief section: 'the real hurdle... you have to believe the agentic layer is worth investing into. If you don't believe your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked' (41:15–41:18); career defensibility: 'it would be crazy for anyone in your organization to conceive of letting you go' (~43:00).
(44:12–44:35) ZTE run check: review phase screenshots posted — background is green, validation shipped one minute ago; documentation phase completes (44:32).

(45:50–48:30) THE SECRET, stated twice (45:58–46:10) + the composable-primitives slide (46:05); SDLC 'a remnant of the past' (46:26); 'the one way is the way that ships in your codebase' (~47:30); recap of the stack: one agent, one prompt, one purpose; orchestrating intelligence (48:17).

quotes.text: You'll witness something most engineers dismiss as impossible: a codebase that nearly runs itself.

This isn't black and white. It's not in loop versus out loop. It's in loop moving toward out loop.

We're not solving the problem directly anymore... the rate in which you can solve your specific problem can now be drastically scaled up when you put your effort into your agentic layer.

prerequisites_tools: TAC 1–6 concepts assumed: agentic prompts, templates/plans (TAC-3), PITER + ADWs (TAC-4), closed loops/testing/review (TAC-5), one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose + conditional docs (TAC-6)
Claude Code CLI (invoked programmatically as `claude -p` with stream-json output)
GitHub CLI (gh) authenticated; a GitHub repo with issues enabled (GITHUB_REPO_URL; optional GITHUB_PAT for a bot account)
Python + uv (all ADW scripts are uv single-file scripts); Node + Bun for the client
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for programmatic Claude Code; OpenAI and/or Anthropic keys for the demo app's NL→SQL
Optional: cloudflared tunnel token (webhook exposure), Cloudflare R2 credentials (screenshot uploads), E2B key (cloud-sandbox PoC), Playwright MCP (review/E2E)
what_student_must_internalize: The velocity scale has three levels — in-loop, out-loop, ZTE — measured by presence: continuous → two touchpoints (prompt + review) → one (prompt only).
ZTE is PITER minus the R: same prompt input, trigger, environment — review is embedded into the pipeline (tests + agentic review + gates) instead of performed by you.
The move to ZTE is evidence-gated per problem class: KPIs (attempts=1, rising streak) prove your review stopped adding value for that class. It is never a global switch.
Parallel agents need isolation: worktree + branch + ports + state per run. The specific isolation tech (worktrees, Docker, VMs, E2B) is interchangeable; the capability is not.
State objects (adw_state.json) are how single-purpose agents compose into pipelines without sharing a context window — and ship's completeness check turns that state into a go/no-go gate.
Model sets are IDKs for compute allocation: one keyword in the issue re-maps which model each slash command runs — escalate implementation/debugging to opus, keep classification on sonnet.
Review's question is 'is what we built what we asked for?' — proof of value (screenshots, and next: video) posted to your review system, not a human re-test.
Dangerous automation deserves explicit interlocks: the ZTE workflow requires uppercase 'ZTE' to run; lowercase silently downgrades to reviewed SDLC.

The SDLC arrangement is arbitrary packaging. The durable asset is the primitive set — templates, plans, prompts, ADW steps — composed per problem class ('the one way is the way that ships in your codebase').
TAC-6 still holds at scale: one agent, one prompt, one purpose — more precision than stacking everything into one context window.
The bottleneck migrates: stop coding (TAC-1) → your typing was the bottleneck; target ZTE (TAC-7) → your reviewing is next.
The final hurdle is belief backed by measurement: invest, instrument, and let your own KPIs tell you when to drop the review.
common_weak_student_failures: Hearing 'stop reviewing' as a day-one instruction and YOLO-merging real work — skipping the entire evidence ladder (chores first, KPIs, 5-in-a-row streaks) that makes ZTE rational.

The opposite failure: dismissing ZTE because 'my codebase is too complex' — and therefore never instrumenting, never discovering the chore classes that were ZTE-ready today ('how else will you know unless you're trying?').
Cargo-culting git worktrees as the point of the lesson, instead of the capability they demonstrate (N isolated agent environments on demand with per-run ports and state).
Running two ADWs in the same directory / same ports and concluding parallel agents 'don't work' — isolation is step zero (the demo allocates 9100–9114/9200–9214 for a reason).
Ignoring state: hand-running adw_build_iso without the plan phase's state and hitting 'No state found' / ship's missing-fields abort, then blaming the tool.
model_set heavy on everything 'to be safe' — paying opus prices for classification and branch naming that the map deliberately keeps on sonnet.
Assuming E2E browser tests ran during SDLC/ZTE — both orchestrators hardcode --skip-e2e; unit tests gate the pipeline, E2E is a separate adw_test_iso run.
Typing 'adw_sdlc_zte_iso' in lowercase and reading the resulting reviewed SDLC run as a bug instead of the uppercase safety interlock working as designed.
Treating the review agent's screenshots as decoration — never opening them, so the review system never earns trust, so presence never drops.
Believing ship uses gh pr merge --squash because the README says so; the code performs a manual --no-ff merge + push (docs drift is itself a lesson: verify countable claims against code).
Skipping worktree cleanup (purge_tree.sh) until the disk fills with full repo copies.
Consuming the lesson as motivation and changing nothing — the lesson's own ask is concrete: pick one chore class this week and encode it end to end.
teach_back_prompt: Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) the three levels of the Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale and the presence number at each level; (2) what PITER → PITE means mechanically — which element is removed and what replaces it inside the pipeline (name at least three gates the tac-7 ZTE workflow enforces before merging); (3) how five agents ran on one machine without colliding — name the four isolation ingredients (worktree, branch, ports, state) and where each lives on disk; (4) what model sets are and why only eight commands escalate to opus; and (5) the secret of TAC — why Dan calls the SDLC 'a remnant of the past' and what he says the durable unit actually is. Finish by resolving the arc: how does 'stop coding' from lesson 1 lead inevitably to 'stop reviewing' in lesson 7?

retrieval_questions.q: Name the three levels of the Agentic Engineering Velocity Scale and your presence at each.
retrieval_questions.a: In-loop (continuous presence, interactive prompting), out-loop (presence of two: prompt + review), zero-touch engineering (presence of one: prompt only).

Target Zero-Touch Engineering — build ADWs so reliable that human review becomes a bottleneck, then remove it and let agents ship prompt-to-production. It's a North Star you target per problem class, not a switch.

retrieval_questions.q: What does PITER become under ZTE and why?
retrieval_questions.a: PITE — the R (review) is dropped because review is embedded in the pipeline (tests, agentic review with screenshots, state validation) instead of performed by a human.

retrieval_questions.q: What four things isolate one ADW run from another in tac-7?
retrieval_questions.a: Its own git worktree (trees/<adw_id>, a full repo copy), its own branch ({class}-issue-{n}-adw-{id}-{slug}), its own ports (backend 9100–9114, frontend 9200–9214, derived from the ADW ID; 15 concurrent slots), and its own state file (agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json).

retrieval_questions.q: List the ten fields of adw_state.json.
retrieval_questions.a: adw_id, issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class, worktree_path, backend_port, frontend_port, model_set, all_adws.

retrieval_questions.q: What phases does adw_sdlc_zte_iso run, and which failure does NOT block shipping?
retrieval_questions.a: Plan → build → test → review → document → ship. Test or review failure aborts ZTE; documentation failure only warns — the run continues to ship.

retrieval_questions.q: How does the ship phase actually merge to main?
retrieval_questions.a: It validates all eight required state fields and the worktree, then in the main repo root: git fetch, checkout main, pull, git merge --no-ff <feature-branch>, git push origin main. (The adws/README's 'approve PR + squash' description is stale — the code does a manual no-ff merge.)

retrieval_questions.q: What safety interlock guards the ZTE workflow at the trigger level?
retrieval_questions.a: The /classify_adw prompt refuses to select adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso unless 'ZTE' is explicitly uppercase in the issue text; lowercase 'zte' downgrades to the reviewed adw_sdlc_iso.

retrieval_questions.q: What is a model set, and which commands escalate on 'heavy'?
retrieval_questions.a: An information-dense keyword (model_set base|heavy) stored in state that re-maps each slash command's model via SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP. On heavy, 8 of 18 commands switch sonnet→opus: /implement, /resolve_failed_test, /resolve_failed_e2e_test, /document, /chore, /bug, /feature, /patch. Classification, testing, review, commit, PR plumbing stay on sonnet.

retrieval_questions.q: What question does the review step answer, and how does it prove its answer?
retrieval_questions.a: 'Is what we built what we asked for?' (not 'does it work' — tests answered that). It drives the app in the worktree via Playwright MCP, takes 1–5 numbered screenshots of critical paths, classifies issues as skippable/tech_debt/blocker, uploads screenshots to Cloudflare R2, and posts them on the GitHub issue.

retrieval_questions.q: How do the agentic KPIs tell you a problem class is ZTE-ready?
retrieval_questions.a: Attempts pinned at 1, streak (consecutive runs with attempts ≤ 2) climbing, size scaling up — while your reviews stop catching anything. Dan's threshold sketch: ~90% confidence a class ships with no issues, 'and that number keeps going up.'

retrieval_questions.q: Which two triggers can start ADWs, and what prevents infinite webhook loops?
retrieval_questions.a: A FastAPI webhook (POST /gh-webhook, port 8001, instant) and a cron poller (every 20 seconds). Every bot comment embeds the [ADW-AGENTS] identifier, and the webhook ignores any payload containing it.

retrieval_questions.q: Do browser E2E tests run inside adw_sdlc_iso / adw_sdlc_zte_iso?
retrieval_questions.a: No — both orchestrators hardcode --skip-e2e ('Always skip E2E tests in SDLC workflows'). Unit tests gate the pipeline; E2E runs only via a standalone adw_test_iso without the flag.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the secret of Tactical Agentic Coding?
retrieval_questions.a: It's not about the software developer lifecycle at all — it's about composable agentic primitives you can use to solve any engineering problem class. The SDLC arrangement is 'completely arbitrary... a package to deliver a message'; the one way is the way that ships in your codebase.

retrieval_questions.q: What does Dan say is the real hurdle of TAC, and his four postures toward the future?
retrieval_questions.a: Belief — 'you have to believe the agentic layer is worth investing into... if you don't believe your agents can run your codebase, you're cooked.' Postures: run away, stand still, move toward it, or sprint ('sprint into the future').

retrieval_questions.q: What committed evidence in the tac-7 repo shows ZTE actually ran?
retrieval_questions.a: specs/issue-47-adw-cc73faf1-...md carries the trigger '/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso - update Upload Data to be Upload'; app/client/index.html ships the changed 'Upload' button; app_docs/agentic_kpis.md records the run (attempts 1, presence 1.0); app_docs/ carries five agent-written feature docs and agents/ holds real run states and logs.

codebase_map.layout_counts: 14 top-level ADW workflow scripts + 9 adw_modules + 2 triggers + 6 adw_tests; 27 slash commands + 6 e2e command specs (33 total .md under .claude/commands); 7 hook scripts; 5 ai_docs; 5 committed app_docs feature docs + agentic_kpis.md; 1 committed spec; 5 committed agents/ run dirs.

what_each_does.adws/adw_sdlc_zte_iso.py: The lesson's headline artifact: chains plan→build→test→review→document→ship via subprocess, one shared ADW ID and state. Test/review failure aborts with a 'ZTE Aborted' comment; documentation failure warns but continues; success posts 'Code has been automatically shipped to production!' and reminds you to purge_tree.sh.
what_each_does.adws/adw_ship_iso.py: The final gate: requires adw-id, validates all 8 state fields are non-null and the worktree exists, then manual merge in repo root (fetch → checkout main → pull → merge --no-ff → push) with original-branch restore on every failure path.
what_each_does.adws/adw_sdlc_iso.py: The reviewed SDLC: plan→build→test→review→document, no ship. Hardcodes --skip-e2e into the test phase.
what_each_does.adws/adw_plan_iso.py: Entry-point workflow: fetches the issue, allocates ports, classifies (/classify_issue), generates the branch name, creates the worktree from origin/main, runs /install_worktree inside it, builds the spec with the issue-class command, commits, pushes, opens the PR — updating state at every step.
what_each_does.adws/adw_patch_iso.py: Lightweight alternative to full SDLC for small fixes ('adw_patch' keyword): worktree + targeted patch plan (specs/patch/) + implement + PR. Used on-video for the CSV-text bug.
what_each_does.adws/adw_modules/worktree_ops.py: create_worktree (git worktree add -b from origin/main), three-way validate_worktree, deterministic get_ports_for_adw (base-36 hash % 15 → 9100+i/9200+i), socket availability checks, .ports.env writer. Latent bug: remove_worktree's fallback calls shutil.rmtree without importing shutil.
what_each_does.adws/adw_modules/agent.py: The programmable Claude Code wrapper: SLASH_COMMAND_MODEL_MAP (18 commands × base/heavy), model resolution from state, prompt logging, `claude -p --model X --output-format stream-json --verbose [--mcp-config] --dangerously-skip-permissions` with cwd=worktree, JSONL parsing, retry ladder [1,3,5]s.
what_each_does.adws/adw_modules/state.py: ADWState: agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json persistence, pydantic-validated 10-field schema, all_adws append tracking, get_working_directory() returning worktree_path when isolated, stdin/stdout piping support.
what_each_does.adws/adw_modules/workflow_ops.py: Shared ops: extract_adw_info via /classify_adw, classify_issue (/chore|/bug|/feature), build_plan, implement_plan, create_commit, create_pull_request, ensure_adw_id, find/create branch, AVAILABLE_ADW_WORKFLOWS runtime validation, [ADW-AGENTS]-prefixed issue messaging.
what_each_does.adws/adw_triggers/trigger_webhook.py: FastAPI receiver (port 8001): filters bot comments, requires 'adw_' text, classifies, blocks dependent workflows without adw_id, persists state, posts the detection comment, launches the workflow detached (Popen, start_new_session) to answer GitHub within 10s. /health runs the full system health check.
what_each_does.adws/adw_triggers/trigger_cron.py: Polling alternative: every 20 seconds; fires on new comment-less issues or a latest comment of exactly 'adw'.
what_each_does.adws/adw_modules/r2_uploader.py: Cloudflare R2 uploads for review screenshots (boto3 S3 API); returns public URLs (default domain tac-public-imgs.iddagents.com) that get embedded in issue comments; silently disables without credentials.
what_each_does..claude/commands/classify_adw.md: Extracts {adw_slash_command, adw_id, model_set} as strict JSON from free text; normalizes command variants; carries the uppercase-ZTE interlock.
what_each_does..claude/commands/install_worktree.md: Agent-run environment installer: .ports.env, .env copies + port appends, .mcp.json/playwright config copies with absolute-path rewrites, uv sync, bun install, DB reset, and a full report contract.
what_each_does..claude/commands/in_loop_review.md: The deliberate step back into the loop: fetch + checkout branch, prepare_app (DB reset + start), open localhost for hands-on inspection.
what_each_does..claude/commands/track_agentic_kpis.md: Maintains app_docs/agentic_kpis.md: per-run rows (attempts from all_adws, plan size via wc -l, diff via git diff --shortstat) and summary metrics (current/longest streak with attempts ≤ 2, totals, average presence) — all arithmetic forced through python -c.
what_each_does..claude/commands/review.md: Spec-vs-implementation review: 1–5 numbered screenshots via Playwright MCP, severity taxonomy (skippable/tech_debt/blocker), success = no blockers, strict-JSON output contract ('we'll immediately run JSON.parse()').
what_each_does..claude/commands/conditional_docs.md: Condition → documentation routing table; the document phase appends new feature docs here so future agents self-serve the right context ('this lets our agents scale with the size of our codebase').
what_each_does..claude/settings.json: Interactive-session permissions (deny git push --force / rm -rf) + all seven hook wirings (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Notification, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, UserPromptSubmit).
what_each_does.app_docs/agentic_kpis.md: Committed KPI evidence: run cc73faf1 (issue #47, /chore, attempts 1, plan 39 lines, diff 274/5/10, average presence 1.0, streak 1) — a real ZTE run's paper trail.
what_each_does.specs/issue-47-adw-cc73faf1-sdlc_planner: Committed plan whose metadata preserves the actual ZTE trigger: issue body '/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso - update Upload Data to be Upload'.
what_each_does.app/server/core/llm_processor.py: The demo app's NL→SQL brain (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 / claude-sonnet-4-0 in the shipped snapshot — the target of the on-video 'bump to o4-mini' chore, whose review reported 78 tests passing).
what_each_does.ai_docs/ (5 files): Pinned third-party context for agents: anthropic_quick_start, claude_code_cli_reference, claude_code_sdk, openai_quick_start, e2b (the containerization alternative Dan name-checks).

generated_not_committed.trees/<adw_id>/: Per-run worktrees (full repo copies); gitignored; created by plan/patch entry points, removed by scripts/purge_tree.sh.
generated_not_committed.agents/<adw_id>/** (fresh runs): State, per-agent prompts, raw_output.jsonl/json session logs, reviewer review_img/ screenshots — five historical run dirs are committed as evidence.
generated_not_committed..ports.env / videos/: Per-worktree port config and Playwright video output dirs created by /install_worktree.
generated_not_committed.logs/<session_id>/: Hook logs per Claude Code session (LOG_BASE_DIR).

current_practice_gaps.gap: Hand-rolled worktree orchestration is now a first-class platform feature
current_practice_gaps.why: tac-7 builds worktree isolation from raw git + port arithmetic + an install prompt. Current Claude Code (mid-2026) exposes isolation natively: worktree-isolated subagents/tasks, sandboxed bash, and cloud/remote agent execution; multi-agent fan-out over worktrees is a standard orchestration pattern rather than custom scripting. The lesson's CONCEPT (isolated, parallel, disposable agent environments with per-run state) transfers unchanged — the plumbing you'd write today is smaller.

current_practice_gaps.gap: subprocess claude -p pipelines → Claude Agent SDK
current_practice_gaps.why: adws/adw_modules/agent.py (subprocess, stream-json parsing, retry ladders, session capture) is exactly the layer the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS) now provides with structured outputs, hooks, session management, and error semantics. The ADW architecture maps 1:1; a 2026 rebuild would swap agent.py for the SDK and keep every workflow script's shape.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Reusable engineering as .claude/commands prompt files → Agent Skills
current_practice_gaps.why: tac-7 encodes 33 command prompts discovered by convention. Agent Skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter, on-demand loading, composability) are the current first-class packaging for the same idea — including the conditional_docs.md pattern, which is essentially hand-rolled skill discovery/progressive disclosure.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Model names and model-set economics are period detail
current_practice_gaps.why: The course-era map is sonnet/opus circa mid-2025 (and the demo app bumps gpt-4.1 → o4-mini). Model families have turned over since; the durable idea is the base/heavy KNOB — per-command compute allocation via an IDK stored in state — not any specific model id. Update the map's values, keep its shape.

current_practice_gaps.gap: ZTE guardrails have matured beyond an uppercase check
current_practice_gaps.why: The uppercase-ZTE interlock is a charming era artifact of prompt-level safety. Current practice layers deterministic controls around auto-merge: branch protection + required CI checks, permission modes and hooks gating tool use, environment-scoped credentials, staged deploys/canaries, and merge queues. Dan hints at exactly this evolution in-lesson ('add that key deploy check step, a bunch of deterministic deploy checks... parallelize the review step so three agents have to agree — run the fusion chain on agents').

current_practice_gaps.gap: Review evidence: screenshots → video + richer review products
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson names the gap itself: 'the next most obvious one to build out is video. Have your agents take video, upload it to a cloud bucket, and post the URLs.' The repo's playwright-mcp-config.json already records 1920×1080 video per run, and Dan calls comprehensive review systems 'an entire product category that is important to build out' — which is precisely what agent-review tooling became.

frame_plan.label: zte-shipped-app
frame_plan.why_for_weak_student: The payoff: the production app after `git pull origin main`, wearing the new background the agent shipped — one prompt in, deployed change out, presence of one.

setup: Clone the course repo: git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-7.git && cd tac-7 — then create YOUR OWN GitHub repo and point origin at it (Dan does the equivalent on-video by resetting origin; ADW needs issues + push rights on a repo you own)
Copy .env.sample → .env; set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (and OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC key in app/server/.env for the NL→SQL app); export GITHUB_REPO_URL
Verify tools: claude --version, gh auth status, uv --version, bun --version, git --version (needs worktree support)
Boot the app once yourself: ./scripts/start.sh → http://localhost:5173; upload sample data; run one NL query; ./scripts/stop_apps.sh
Read .claude/settings.json and adws/README.md; say out loud what a workflow may do and where its evidence will land (agents/, trees/, the issue thread)
reproduce_dan: File an issue: 'Add a footer with the current table count. adw_sdlc_iso' — run `cd adws && uv run adw_sdlc_iso.py <issue#>` (manual mode first; webhook optional)
While it runs, verify isolation: `git worktree list` shows trees/<adw_id>; cat trees/<adw_id>/.ports.env; cat agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json and name all ten fields
Jump into the agent's environment mid-run like Dan: `code trees/<adw_id>` and watch the branch in the status bar
When it finishes, audit the evidence chain on the issue: classification → state JSON → plan path → test summary → review summary + screenshots → documentation → PR; open the PR diff
Go in-loop deliberately: in claude, run /in_loop_review <branch-name>; manually exercise the feature in the browser; note what your review caught (likely: nothing)

Fire a heavy run: new issue 'Generate random rows for a selected table. adw_sdlc_iso model_set heavy' — then prove the knob worked by checking which model the implementor ran (agents/<id>/sdlc_implementor/raw_output.jsonl model field, or the issue's Model Set line)
Run a patch-class fix: issue 'Rename the Query button to Run. adw_patch_iso' and compare its footprint (specs/patch/, phases run) to full SDLC

ZTE ceremony: issue '/chore adw_sdlc_ZTE_iso - change the background color to light green' (uppercase ZTE). Watch all six phases; confirm the merge landed with git pull && git log --oneline -3 (merge commit 'via ADW Ship workflow') and the app shows the change from main
Prove the interlock: repeat with lowercase 'adw_sdlc_zte_iso' and confirm the classifier downgrades it to reviewed adw_sdlc_iso (no auto-merge)
Read app_docs/agentic_kpis.md after your runs; recompute attempts and streak by hand from all_adws and check the table agrees
Clean up every run: ./scripts/purge_tree.sh <adw_id>; confirm `git worktree list` is clean
stretch: Parallel proof: file two independent chores and launch both ADWs back to back; capture `git worktree list` and both .ports.env files while both run; explain why they can't collide (worktree, branch, ports, state)
Port-collision drill: occupy a run's deterministic port (python3 -m http.server 9107) before launching; find in the logs where find_next_available_ports picked the fallback slot
Break ship's gate on purpose: run adw_plan_iso only, then adw_ship_iso <issue#> <adw-id>; screenshot the missing-fields abort listing exactly which state fields were null

Docs-vs-code audit (technical-accuracy drill): adws/README.md claims ship 'approves the PR and merges using squash'. Read adw_ship_iso.py and write three sentences on what it actually does (--no-ff manual merge + push) and how you'd detect the difference from git log
Find the latent bug in worktree_ops.remove_worktree (shutil.rmtree without import); explain the failure path and why validate_worktree's three-way check still keeps pipelines honest

E2E honesty check: prove from adw_sdlc_zte_iso.py that E2E is always skipped in SDLC/ZTE, then run E2E yourself: uv run adw_test_iso.py <issue#> <adw-id> (no --skip-e2e) with Playwright MCP configured

Extend the review system one step toward Dan's 'next most obvious' idea: playwright-mcp-config.json already records video — locate the worktree's videos/ dir after a review and post the file path (or an uploaded URL) back to the issue

Wire the real trigger: uv run adw_triggers/trigger_webhook.py + scripts/expose_webhook.sh (cloudflared) + a repo webhook for Issues/Issue comments; file an issue from your phone and stay out of the loop
pass_criteria: One adw_sdlc_iso run completed end to end from a GitHub issue with zero hand-typed application code; issue thread shows classification, state, plan, test, review (with ≥1 screenshot), documentation, and a PR
You can print agents/<adw_id>/adw_state.json and explain every one of the ten fields, including why ship refuses to run when any of its eight required fields is null
A heavy-set run demonstrably used opus for implementation while classification stayed on sonnet (evidence from raw_output.jsonl or the issue thread)
One uppercase-ZTE run merged to main with a 'via ADW Ship workflow' merge commit AND one lowercase 'zte' attempt visibly downgraded to reviewed SDLC
Two ADW runs executed concurrently with disjoint worktrees, branches, and port pairs (evidence captured)
app_docs/agentic_kpis.md updated by your runs; you recomputed attempts/streak/presence by hand and they match

All worktrees purged afterward; git worktree list clean; you can state Tactic #7, the three velocity-scale levels with presence numbers, PITER→PITE, and the secret (composable agentic primitives) without notes

confidence_notes: Quotes cross-checked against the 11,194-line VTT; timestamps accurate to ±5s (cue-boundary rounding). Auto-transcript mishears normalized: 'Pete not Peter' = PITE not PITER, 'Peter framework' = PITER, '04 many/mini' = o4-mini, 'tack/text seven' = TAC-7, 'agent decoding/logistic coding' = agentic coding, 'yellow mode' = yolo mode, 'heavy forward opus' = heavy → opus.
PITE spelling verified against the on-screen course tactic card at 31:52 ('Go from PITER to PITE with one prompt agentic workflows'), not just audio.
Naming duality verified in artifacts: tactic = Zero-Touch Engineering (course card); code/docstrings/comments = Zero Touch Execution (adw_sdlc_zte_iso.py, GitHub comments). Both recorded.

All countable claims verified on disk under tac/tac-7: 14 adw_*.py workflow scripts; 27+6 command .md files; 7 hooks; 10 state fields; 18-command model map with exactly 8 heavy→opus entries; ports 9100–9114/9200–9214 (15 slots); retry delays [1,3,5]s; cron poll 20s; webhook port 8001.

Doc/code drifts found and flagged (do not repeat them in the chapter): adws/README says ship 'approves PR + squash' — code does manual --no-ff merge + push (Dan's narration matches the CODE); README's branch-name example lacks the issue-/adw- prefixes the code and committed artifacts use; remove_worktree has an unimported shutil fallback.
Both SDLC orchestrators (adw_sdlc_iso.py, adw_sdlc_zte_iso.py) hardcode --skip-e2e — verified in source; E2E runs only via standalone adw_test_iso.

On-video runs vs committed snapshot distinguished: video issues #51 (drop zone), #52 (JSON export), random-data (heavy), #54 (o4-mini; review reported 78 tests passing), CSV-text patch, and ZTE #62 (background color, shipped green on-screen at 49:14) are NOT in the distributed repo's committed state; the snapshot instead carries earlier run evidence (issues 3, 9, 15, 47 → five app_docs feature docs incl. light-sky-blue #E0F6FF and the shipped 'Upload' button, one spec, agents/ dirs, agentic_kpis.md with presence 1.0). Issue numbers cited only where frame-verified (#51, #52, #54, #62).
